patients with carcinoma prostate, treated with estrogen for a long time, have an impaired but slowly increasing pituitary function.

1) serum levels of testosterone and gonadotrophins (FSH and LH) are lower in patients with prostatic cancer treated by long-term estrogen treatment than in untreated patients; 2) serum levels of FSH and LH increase in all patients after orchiectomy; 3) serum testosterone levels are higher in long-term estrogen treated patients than in untreated patients after orchiectomies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of estrogen treatment for prostatc carcinoma on the pituitar-gonadal axis and on prolactin levels.
the pituitary function of patients with prostatic cancer, who are either treated by primary orchidectomy, or by orchidectomy after previous estrogen therapy for less than 2 or more than 3 years.
the pituitary function in patients with prostatic cancer, treated with orchiectomy, with or without previous estrogen treatment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

patients with prostatic cancer treated for a long time with estrogens have a lower pituitary function than patients treated with estrogens for a shorter period of time or not treated with estrogons at all.
the pituitary function in patients with prostatic cancer is impaired by long-term estrogen treatment.
the pituitary-gonadal axis in long-term estrogen-treated men with carcinoma of the prostatic gland does not recover completely after orchiectomy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the pituitary function in patients treated with long-term estrogens was impaired, but the pituitary response to the orchiectomy was not significantly different from that of patients treated by primary surgery.

patients with prostate cancer treated with estrogen for longer than 3 yr, have an impaired but slowly increasing pituitary gland response, which may explain the lack of response to orchiectomy in this group of patients.
the pituitary gonadotropin secretion is impaired by estrogen treatment of prostatic carcinoma, and the impairment may persist for years after discontinuation of the treatment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of the word “hypo” is not necessarily synonymous with a low testosterone level, and it should not be used to diagnose hypogonadism in men with symptoms suggestive of testosterone deficiency.
the use of testosterone in men with prostate cancer is not a simple matter of giving a man a testosterone supplement and hoping that the cancer goes away.
it is not just about what we do but how we do it that matters.
